title: Hundreds of IDF investigations into killings without public outcome, BBC Verify finds
content: BBC Verify has identified 254 incidents in which the Israeli military has been accused of killing or injuring people in Gaza, Lebanon, the occupied West Bank and Israel that it said it was investigating, but have no public outcome. Using purpose-built AI tools, BBC Verify combed through more than 60,000 news reports and examined hundreds of incidents in which the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) faced allegations of harm since the start of the Gaza war. Following extensive manual checking of each incident, we found 300 cases that the military said it was looking into, only 28 of which had outcomes published on the IDF website. For a further 18 incidents it was unclear if the investigation has been concluded. BBC Verify approached the IDF about each case multiple times but only received information on two incidents, which the IDF said are still under review. "The IDF takes every allegation or report raising concerns about conduct that may be inconsistent with the law or IDF directives with the utmost seriousness," it said in a statement. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), which works in warzones to uphold the Geneva Conventions, publishes guidelines that state investigations into potential violations of international humanitarian law, whether criminal or otherwise, should be as transparent as possible. Of the 254 incidents identified by BBC Verify, 158 occurred in Gaza, 48 in the West Bank and 32 in Lebanon. A further 16 took place in Israel or in IDF detention. All happened between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026, and at least one person was reportedly killed in more than 200 of them. Some of the incidents without public outcomes date back to late 2023. One of the deadliest cases involved a strike on a school building in Gaza in August 2024 when at least 93 people were reportedly killed, including six women and 11 children. For three years, the Israeli military has often responded to accusations of harm by stating an incident is being investigated in some form, for example that it is being "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". Often, that is the last that is heard about a case. A number of incidents have been escalated for criminal investigation by the IDF. Two that came under intense public scrutiny involved the killings of five-year-old Hind Rajab, and of 15 Palestinian Red Crescent emergency workers who were shot more than 100 times and allegedly targeted at close range. The results of IDF military investigations are not routinely made public, including those leading to criminal investigations of its soldiers. A number that have been published relate to hostages in Gaza who were allegedly killed as a result of Israeli operations. In some cases, the military has only announced it is investigating an incident after being approached by BBC Verify or other media organisations. In August, the IDF published a rare report detailing internal probes into five incidents in Gaza, including the killings of Hind Rajab and the 15 Palestinian emergency workers, which it revealed had been escalated to criminal investigations. In the three other cases, which involved the killings of seven aid workers from the World Central Kitchen (WCK) in an air strike and the killing of four Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) aid workers in two separate Gaza attacks, the IDF said it did not find a basis for or reasonable suspicion to begin a criminal investigation. The report also stated Israel's General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM), which handles IDF investigations into "exceptional operational incidents" , had completed the review of approximately 150 cases since the start of the war. These cases have now been transferred to the IDF's Military Prosecution for examination, according to the report. The IDF did not outline what the 150 incidents were, and did not clarify whether they were separate to the cases identified by BBC Verify when asked. Despite multiple requests, the IDF has not provided a transparent breakdown of the status of the 300 investigations identified by BBC Verify. In a statement, the IDF said it "publishes information regarding the outcomes of investigations and examinations when possible, subject to legal and operational considerations, as well as restrictions relating to privacy and information security". It added that certain incidents are examined through command-level operational reviews, which are "intended to establish the sequence of events, identify failures and draw lessons for the purpose of improving operational conduct and taking any necessary command measures". The IDF also said that during the war it has taken disciplinary action in dozens of cases against soldiers who failed to meet the standards expected of them and acted contrary to IDF directives, including being removed from combat positions and from reserve service. Freedom of Information data obtained by Yesh Din, an Israeli human rights group, showed that between October 2023 and August 2024 at least 1,456 Gaza-related incidents were referred to the FFAM. Twelve of these reviews were completed and referred to the Military Advocate General (MAG) Corps, two of which resulted in criminal investigations. Dan Owen, a researcher at Yesh Din which has been monitoring military investigations since 2006, told BBC Verify that he believes the IDF will often try to "prolong" investigations. "They try to stretch out these processes to the point where people forget and people don't care about them," he said. Janina Dill, a professor of international law at the University of Oxford, said that according to the Geneva Conventions a party to armed conflict has a responsibility to "investigate and potentially prosecute its own". "That's the absolute clear bottom line," she added. "There are also guidelines for investigation, endorsed by the ICRC, so they have some authority. And they emphasise promptness, thoroughness, impartiality." Eran Shamir-Borer, director of the Center for Security and Democracy at the Israeli Democracy Institute (IDI) and a former top lawyer for the IDF, said there are "genuine challenges" investigating allegations in conflicts Israel is involved in, given the complex combat environments. "[In] a territory which is hostile, not always under your control, collecting evidence could be very challenging. Lots of forces on the ground, many of them executing fire," he said. Shamir-Borer added: "The idea of investigating soldiers in the context of a war is never a popular thing to do," which he said is also seen in other law abiding countries. He added that Israel would only benefit from being more transparent about its investigations, and he would encourage the IDF to be "more forthcoming with information that they are sharing with the public on the progress they are making in investigating various allegations". Since the Hamas-led attacks in Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage, the IDF has carried out extensive military operations in Gaza which it said aimed to bring back the hostages and dismantle Hamas. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the war, according to the Hamas-run health ministry. BBC Verify has reported on the killing of emergency workers and people trying to access aid inside Gaza, the levelling of thousands of buildings in the strip and incidents of alleged misconduct carried out by Israeli soldiers over the last three years. Just two months into the war, two women were killed by Israeli troops in the only Catholic church in the territory in December 2023, during an incident that the IDF later said was under review. A mother, Nahida Anton, and her daughter, Samar Anton, were killed by sniper fire inside the grounds of the Holy Family church in Gaza, according to the Latin Patriarchate of Jerusalem. BBC Verify contacted the IDF about the report at the time. The military said that an initial review suggested troops had been operating against a Hamas threat they had identified "in the area of the church". The IDF added that it was "conducting a thorough review of the incident". In September 2025, BBC Verify asked for an update on the review and was told that the incident was "still being reviewed by the FFAM". Now, almost three years since Nahida and Samar were killed, the IDF has again said the incident is under review. Following the latest request for information, the IDF said: "Complex incidents may require considerable time to collect, cross-check, and verify the relevant factual information." It added: "The IDF does not shorten or forgo examination or investigative procedures in order to meet external timelines." One of the deadliest incidents that remains under investigation by the Israeli military is an air strike carried out on a school building in eastern Gaza city in August 2024. The Hamas-run civil defence agency said at least 93 people, including six women and 11 children, were killed in the strike on the Tabaeen school complex and nearby mosque. The buildings had been housing displaced Palestinians when multiple Israeli strikes hit the area at the time of dawn prayers. Videos verified by the BBC of the aftermath showed a cloud of dust as emergency workers worked their way through small fires, rubble and body parts strewn on the floor. Photos taken in daylight showed blood-soaked floors, debris and people's clothes scattered around. Experts told BBC Verify munition fragments visible at the scene matched that of a GBU-39 - a precision-guided bomb supplied by the US to the Israeli military. The IDF at the time said a Hamas command and control centre had been embedded in the school building, and that IDF soldiers killed 31 fighters in the incident. It added that according to an "initial review" the casualty numbers did not align with the information held by the IDF, the precise munitions used and the accuracy of the strike. The IDF told BBC Verify this incident remains under review. BBC Verify also looked into incidents the IDF said it was investigating in the West Bank. Israel has occupied the territory since the 1967 war and built dozens of settlements there, which is illegal under international law. More than 1,000 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces since 11 October 2023, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs . BBC Verify examined more than 50 IDF investigations into incidents in the territory, at least 26 of which involved women and children being killed or injured. One of those incidents took place just outside of Jenin in September 2024, when Israeli forces reportedly killed 16-year-old Lujain Musleh during an Israeli operation . Lujain's father said she was shot in the head as she looked out of the window at her house in Kafr Dan, after soldiers had surrounded a neighbouring house. The Israeli military said at the time that armed fighters had fired on the soldiers, who had "fired back at a suspect who observed" them, and that the details of the incident were under review. BBC Verify also found nearly 40 IDF investigations into incidents of harm in Lebanon. The Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah fired rockets into Israel in support of Hamas following the 7 October attacks. Israel has since launched two major invasions into Lebanon, where more than 4,000 people have been killed according to the country's health authorities. One IDF investigation identified by BBC Verify took place on 10 November 2024. An Israeli strike killed 23 people, including seven children , near the city of Byblos, according to the Lebanese health ministry. Verified footage of the aftermath showed smoke rising between rubble and warped metal strewn across the ground where buildings had been destroyed. The IDF said at the time it had targeted a site where Hezbollah had been operating from and storing weapons, and that the incident was under review. Michael Schmitt is a professor of international law at the University of Reading who has previously worked closely with the IDF. He said the Israeli military's legal division is the "gold standard in terms of understanding the law", and added that "every allegation that there was a violation does not necessarily trigger a full-blown investigation". Schmitt said there can be a number of reasons why the IDF may be unable to publicly reveal the details of an investigation or a decision not to pursue one. "For example, you do not want to reveal operational details or particular rules of engagement because the enemy forces will adapt," he said, adding: "And even if you did pursue an investigation, many elements of [it] would remain confidential." Dill, who is also a co-director of the Oxford Institute for Ethics, Law and Armed Conflict (ELAC), said: "Three years into this operation, some of these investigations should have been concluded." She said that when it comes to investigating incidents of harm, "Israel has relied heavily on the argument that it is a rule-of-law country to delegitimatise attempts by the international community to investigate". "If we have cases of documented abuse that either don't get investigated or the investigations get stuck, and we have reasonable grounds to believe that they get kicked into the long grass, then that would undermine the narrative that Israel is fully capable of taking care of providing accountability," she added. BBC Verify gathered 61,000 reports from BBC News and Reuters which mentioned Gaza, the West Bank or Lebanon, published between 7 October 2023 and 19 August 2026. We built an AI search engine to look through those reports for incidents where people may have been injured or killed by Israeli forces, and where the IDF said the report was being investigated, or for example "looked into", "reviewed", "checked" or "examined". This identified almost 5,000 reports. Each one was manually checked by BBC Verify reporters, who excluded any which did not meet the criteria above. This left 1,343 reports of incidents that the IDF said it was looking into. Some of these reports described the same incidents. We built another AI tool to remove these duplicate reports. It grouped reports into unique incidents based on the publication date, incident date, location, and numbers reported injured or killed. We then manually checked that each report had been assigned to the correct group, leaving us with 300 unique incidents. For each of these incidents we then manually checked our records including the incident date, location, and how many people were killed or injured against the original BBC News or Reuters report. We shared the details of each case with the IDF including the incident date, location, the news report describing the incident, and the IDF's original comment indicating it was looking into the matter. We asked the IDF for comment and the latest status of each case. The IDF did not say whether any of these investigations had concluded in response to the BBC's requests. For each incident we also looked for statements on the IDF's website suggesting that the investigation had been concluded, using two different AI assisted web search engines. We found evidence that 28 cases were closed based on statements detailing the findings or indicating that no further steps would be taken. For a further 18 incidents, it was unclear whether the investigation had been concluded. This included cases where the IDF published initial information about the incident without a clear indication it was closed, and cases where the IDF had characterised some or all of the people killed or injured as combatants, in statements on its own website. This left us with at least 254 incidents of harm the Israeli military had said it was looking into, for which we did not find a public outcome on the IDF's website. This was not an exhaustive search, and it is likely that there are more investigations into incidents of harm that were not captured in our search. Additional reporting by Barbara Metzler. Targets allegedly included the Israeli embassy and consulate, a woman said to be of interest to Iran, a college, and Britain's oldest synagogue. Israel said in September it would act in response to UK sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The consulate, first established in 1838, was set to be closed by the Israeli government in retaliation for UK sanctions. title: Australian woman charged with lacing colleague's curry with snail poison
content: An Australian woman has been charged after allegedly lacing a colleague's curry with snail poison. Police in the state of Western Australia say the alleged victim made a meal for her co-workers in February, which they shared at morning tea. But when the 58-year-old returned to eat leftovers at lunch, she noticed bright green granules in the food and that her tongue felt numb after tasting it. The accused - who was in a relationship with the alleged victim - has been charged with endangering the life, health or safety of another person after a months-long investigation, and will face court on 5 November. Police allege the 43-year-old woman - who hasn't been named - visited a chemical storage shed before returning to the staffroom where the curry was kept. After tasting it, the alleged victim handed the meal over to detectives, who identified the substance as snail pellets containing metaldehyde, a poisonous substance. Commissioner Col Blanch told reporters the poison can cause serious injury or death. "We're just very thankful that the person who tasted the curry was aware of something that wasn't quite right," he said, according to the Seven Network. Farmers report thousands of mice per hectare destroying crops and invading homes. Steven Mattaboni, 38, died on Saturday after a shark attack while spearfishing at Rottnest Island. title: What if you could turn off your algorithm? Australia is about to try
content: New legislation is being tabled in Australia's parliament on Thursday to force big tech to allow users to switch off algorithms which send them recommended content - but it's not the first country to try. The BBC's Tiffanie Turnbull in Sydney explains what is being proposed. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has apologised for remarks he made about popstar Kylie Minogue in a podcast interview last week. US supporters were delighted after their team won 2-0 against the Socceroos while Australian fans were left disappointed but still hopeful. Crops are being ravaged and homes are being invaded by the rodents - and it’s costing farmers hundreds of thousands of dollars. Almost 90 drones fell from the sky over Sydney's Darling Harbour during a popular winter light show. The BBC's Katy Watson explains the case, the cultural sensitivities and why it has caused so much anger. The Hollywood star is accused by fellow Australian actress Charlotte MacInnes of making defamatory statements. Two-up is a coin toss betting game that was played by Australian soldiers during World War One - it’s now only legal across Australia on 25 April. The boy, who was uninjured, was dragged for 350 metres after the back doors trapped his arm and school bag. BBC News journalist Simon Atkinson explains how the couple's tour will be different compared to their last visit. The BBC spoke to people in Sydney to hear their thoughts on the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s trip to Australia. Fugitive Dezi Freeman has been wanted since he shot dead two police officers on his rural property in August last year. Three months since it came into effect, teenagers tell the BBC how the world-first law has impacted their lives so far. Passengers discovered a real possum nestled among other native Australian toy animals at Hobart Airport, Tasmania. For 25 years, a rural Australian town has been transforming its main street into an inland beach. Austin Appelbee, 13, swam to get help for his mother and siblings after they were swept out to sea. People were seen running away as soon as they came across the venomous snake. The BBC spoke to people in Sydney about the four shark attacks in 48 hours along Australia's New South Wales coast. Heavy rain did not dampen a man's spirits as he decided to take a dive into a flooded Sydney golf course. Australia's Great Ocean Road closed on Thursday after flash floods hit the state of Victoria. title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
content: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. "Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. "The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. And the dangers extend beyond flooding. A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. "One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. "What happened after that no one knows," he added. Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes. "These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group. But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved. One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value. "What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank. Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders. The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow. "There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD. He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks. Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay. "Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says. Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat. Authorities in South East Asia have turned to weather modification as fires blanket the region in smog. Thick orange smog descended on the Indonesian city of Palangka Raya as wildfires continue raging nearby. China is the North's largest trading partner and a lifeline against the sanctions Pyongyang faces. title: North Korea and China open new bridge after 12-year delay
content: A long-delayed road bridge linking China and North Korea has opened, Chinese state media report, as trade ties improve between the neighbours. China is North Korea's largest trading partner and a lifeline against heavy international sanctions over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme. The New Yalu River Bridge spans 3km (1.9 miles) from the Chinese border city of Dandong to Sinuiju in North Korea, and is set to become the main land route for trade between them. Its launch, initially slated for 2014, had been indefinitely postponed after North Korea halted construction of its roads and customs facilities, as relations with Beijing turned frosty. The New Yalu River Bridge is an alternative to the decades-old Sino-Korean Friendship Bridge, which was built between 1937 and 1943 during Imperial Japan's occupation of the region. It is an "important facility for connectivity" between the two countries, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday, adding that the route would "further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges". Last year, bilateral trade reached $2.7bn, marking a recovery to pre-pandemic levels, mostly fuelled by Chinese exports to North Korea. A sharp and sudden increase in trade across the border is "unlikely" as the UN sanctions on North Korea remain in effect, Kang Jun-young, a professor of Chinese studies at the Hankuk University of Foreign Studies, tells the BBC. "Pyongyang is also wary of a sudden flood of Chinese imports that would greatly expand China's influence over its domestic market," he adds. "China is well aware of these concerns, so trade is more likely to grow gradually." Beijing and Pyongyang are long-standing allies with a mutual defence treaty, the only one that China has with any country. The relationship is often described "as close as lips and teeth", a remark first made by China's former leader Mao Zedong. But the alliance is not without tension. Ties were frosty for much of the 2010s as Beijing's patience over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons programme wore thin. Kim Jong Un conducted a nuclear test in 2017 and has since ramped up tests of banned ballistic missiles - all of which increased US wariness, and strengthened its military alliances with South Korea and Japan. China's attitude has shifted more recently. "Whilst only a decade ago, Beijing was overtly critical of North Korea's nuclearisation - and indeed calling for Pyongyang's denuclearisation - China is now saying little, if anything, to this effect," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford, tells the BBC. Observers say one reason is that North Korea has grown closer to Russia because of the Ukraine war. At least 2,300 North Korean soldiers are believed to have died fighting for Russia in Ukraine. In return, Russia supplies North Korea with oil, in violation of UN sanctions. In 2024, Russia was estimated to have sent more than a billion barrels of oil as payment for Pyongyang's weapons and troops. Last month, North Korea and Russia opened their first road bridge, which Russian state media said would allow the movement of up to 300 vehicles and more than 2,000 people every day. So Beijing is believed to be trying to reassert its sway over Pyongyang by rekindling ties. Air China resumed direct flights between Beijing and Pyongyang in March after a six-year hiatus triggered by the pandemic. The two countries reopened passenger train services the same month. Chinese President Xi Jinping's first state visit of this year, in June, was to Pyongyang, where he met North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. "The opening of the New Yalu River Bridge demonstrates bilateral relations are improving and that Xi Jinping's June visit to North Korea was more than symbolic," says Leif-Eric Easley, a professor at Ewha University in Seoul. "But the long delay, including North Korea's pandemic self-isolation and domestic socioeconomic crackdowns, shows what a difficult partner Pyongyang can be for Beijing." title: Retired US generals call on Pentagon to cancel 'barbaric' execution livestream
content: A group of 72 retired US generals, admirals, and other high-ranking military officers are pressing the US government to cancel plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. "We ask the President, our Congressional representatives, and our fellow citizens to act to prevent this barbaric abuse of authority," they wrote in a letter where they also argued the livestream would turn the mass killer into a "martyr". Last week, the Pentagon announced it would publicly show the 3 December execution of Nidal Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who shot dead 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base. Lawmakers from both parties, as well as religious leaders, have criticised the plan. Last week President Donald Trump said he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but some administration officials are now leaning against it, according to CBS News, the BBC's US media partner. CBS reported thatTrump had not yet made a final decision on the livestream as of Tuesday. In the open letter released on Wednesday, the former military leaders - which included 45 generals, 12 admirals and several former judge advocates general - said they did not oppose the death penalty being carried out. But they argued a public execution would violate the US Constitution's protections against cruel and unusual punishment and turn what should be a "solemn and grave punishment" into "a carnival for the enjoyment of voyeurs and spectators". "This type of exploitative broadcasting - that debases human dignity- will taint the honor of the military that employs it, and a nation that allows it," they also wrote. "It will be used by our nation's enemies to stoke hatred, harm American soldiers and citizens in the future, and will ensure that Hasan becomes a martyr for attacking and killing his fellow soldiers." The letter's signatories came from throughout the military and included a handful of officers who retired during Trump's first term. Some also had served during the Iraq and Afghanistan wars. Hasan said in court that he carried out the shooting at Fort Hood, the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American base, believing he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. Hasan was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair. Retired Maj Gen Tony Taguba, who led the Army's investigation into reported prisoner abuses at Abu Ghraib in Iraq, and retired Air Force Coll Moe Davis, a prosecutor at the Guatanamo Bay detention centre who called waterboarding torture, signed the letter. So did Charles Bolden, a US Marine Corps Major General who became the head of Nasa, and a retired Lt Gen Claudia Kennedy, the first woman to become a three-star general in the Army. Trump has said he signed off on the execution, but while he approves of the livestream plan, a final decision is yet to be made. It would be the first public execution in the US in almost a century. The plan, which was announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has been heavily criticised by politicians, academics and experts. Katie Zacharia does not appear to be registered to the legal bar in any state where she has lived. title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
content: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual. Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?" Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall. The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000). "Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items. In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable". Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000. They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day. "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity." Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception." When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers. A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual. Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m. The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!" The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them. This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson. The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit. The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird. She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier. But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise. Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here. "I really like it here." Naturalist Martin Gray says it is likely that the young guillemots lacked experience to deal with bad weather. The Royal Borough of Windsor & Maidenhead proposes "to explore new homes for the animals". A sharp increase in human activity is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, studies show. Researchers say the floating device acted as a deterrent for seabirds in the area. title: I'm 12 and I want to try protein powder - should I?
content: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it. In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders. Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder. As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet. So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good? My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis. His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this. "I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says. But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements. "They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them." Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair. But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet. For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS. A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand. If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight. But do teens really need it if they're eating well? For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine. It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients. Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet. There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea. Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor. Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines. "Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says. "And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow." Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants. Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust. He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods. So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost. Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes. During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass. But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein. "If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much." He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded. Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away." The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein." Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly. If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first. Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same. Copyright 2026 BBC. title: Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
content: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities. All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz. The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water. The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday. Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added. Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February. At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time. However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency. One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping. The Windsor Castle state visit will be the first for a Sultan of Oman in the UK since 1982. BBC Security Correspondent Frank Gardner analyses what intelligence agency's boss said in his annual speech and what it means for Britain. The prime minister says Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard "almost certainly" directed the RAF Fairford incident. A £60m investment has seen four of Europe's biggest quay cranes delivered to Southampton docks. title: Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine. Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine. Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed". The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader. BBC World News correspondent Joe Inwood explains what we know about the meeting. Read more about the meeting in London. The big test facing Kemi Badenoch after her conference speech Nigel Farage has been addressing Reform UK members at the party's conference in Birmingham. The PM says he doesn't think his poodle-mix would "get along" with Larry the cat, who has lived at No 10 for 15 years. The new prime minister told Laura Kuenssberg that people "voted for a manifesto" that he would honour, when pressed on whether there will be an early general election. See inside Andy Burnham's first week in charge, with an exclusive behind the scenes look with Laura Kuenssberg. After becoming PM on Monday, Burnham appointed John Healey as chancellor, Ed Miliband as foreign secretary and Wes Streeting as defence secretary The BBC's Annita McVeigh talks us through some key appointments as Andy Burnham takes office. The BBC's Sarah Smith looks at how the new UK prime minister will manage his most crucial, and perhaps the trickiest, international relationship. Andy Burnham has become the UK's prime minister after being appointed by the King at Buckingham Palace. Andy Burnham spoke outside Downing Street after he replaced Keir Starmer as prime minister and leader of the Labour party. Starmer spoke in front of an applauding crowd on Downing Street. title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
content: Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said. Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment. The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka , spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency. Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online. During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad. Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July. It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling. Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September. International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life. "Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday. Authorities in South East Asia have turned to weather modification as fires blanket the region in smog.
